results.title: Baseten review 2026: pricing, Truss, and performance
results.author: 1,490 words
highlights:
Updated August 2026 · 6 min read · 1,490 words

Baseten runs two surfaces. Model APIs serve 13 curated models (DeepSeek V4, GLM 5.2, Kimi K3 and K2.6, Inkling, Nemotron Ultra, gpt-oss 120B) at market rates, with tool calling, structured outputs, and JSON mode on all of them. Dedicated deployments let you push any containerized model with the open-source Truss CLI and bill per GPU minute, from $0.01052 for a T4 to $0.16633 for a B200. Baseten posted the lowest TTFT on the Artificial Analysis provider board in August 2026 at 0.49 seconds.

...

- Two products: a 13-model curated API and a bring-your-own-model platform. Different pricing, different work.
- Model API rates match the market: GLM 5.2 at $1.40 / $4.40, Kimi K3 at $3.00 / $15.00.
- Dedicated GPUs bill per minute, which is unusual and useful. An H100 is $0.10833/min, about $6.50/hour.
- Truss is open source and the dev loop (`truss watch`) syncs local changes in seconds.
- Lowest published time to first token in the category: 0.49 seconds on Inkling Small.
- Endpoints speak both OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages.

### Per-minute GPU pricing

Baseten is the only provider in this comparison that quotes GPUs per minute rather than per hour or per second. The hourly column below is our conversion, not a Baseten figure.

Training runs on the same GPU and CPU rates as deployments, so there is no separate training rate card to reason about. Plans are Basic at $0 pay-as-you-go, Pro with volume discounts, and Enterprise at custom pricing; new accounts get complimentary credits, though Baseten does not publish the amount.

Baseten H100s at an effective $6.50 per hour are well above the compute market: Together clusters are $3.99, Modal works out to about $3.95, and DeepInfra lists $2.20. You are paying for the platform, the autoscaler, and the deployment tooling, not for the silicon. If all you need is silicon, buy it somewhere else.

results.title: The old GPUs everyone expected to get cheaper are renting for more, and Wall Street started calling them collateral · Stacks
results.author: Marc Rubinstein (Net Interest
highlights:
The price of renting a GPU launched in 2020 is going up. For two years the market took it as given that old chips get cheaper every year, and that assumption has now turned over. On the Silicon Data figures Marc Rubinstein cites, an hour of Nvidia H100 time has gone from $1.96 at the end of November to $2.71 now.

A post from the outfit that compiles those figures shows the climb had already begun early this year. An hour that cost $2.00 on December 9, 2025 cost $2.20 four weeks later. At that point A100 and B200 rates held steady, so it looked like a one-generation story.

## At renewal the rate doubles

The gap opens widest at the moment a contract is rewritten.

What Baseten pays now per B200 hour$2.63

The rate after the October renewal$5.10

One renewal lifts the rate by this multiple. What went up in price is not a new chip but a chip already in use.

Net Interest, 2026-08-14, citing Baseten's disclosure, accessed 2026-08-14

Baseten sells software and computing capacity to companies running lower-cost AI models. A tenant absorbing an increase of that size is telling you the same machine is hard to find elsewhere. What actually changed here is not the level but the tenor, the length of time a price is quoted for. Silicon Data now compiles forward rates for delivery in 2027 and 2028, and that curve slopes upward. A forward rate is not what something costs today but what two parties agree today to exchange it for later. It is the equivalent of writing next summer's electricity bill into a contract this morning. The starting point of the article is that a curve exists, not that a price moved.

results.title: Best AI Inference Platforms in 2026: Modal vs Baseten vs Replicate vs Together AI | DevToolLab Blog
results.author: DevToolLab Team
highlights:
As of August 22, 2026, the same NVIDIA H100 costs $3.95/hr on Modal (billed per second), $5.49/hr on Replicate (per second), $5.49/hr on a Together AI dedicated endpoint (per hour), and $6.50/hr on Baseten (per minute), all read from the vendors' own pricing pages the day this was written. That 65% spread on identical silicon is four different bets about what you are really buying: raw seconds, managed replicas, a model catalog, or tokens. Meanwhile the money says this category is the center of gravity: Baseten announced a $1.5 billion Series F at a reported $13 billion valuation in June 2026, and Cloudflare bought Replicate outright.

...

## Baseten

Baseten pricing page with the per-minute toggle selected, showing dedicated deployment rates: T4 at $0.01052, L4 at $0.01414, A10G at $0.02012, A100 at $0.06667, H100 MIG at $0.0625, H100 at $0.10833, and B200 at $0.16633 per minute

Baseten is the production-replica specialist, and the market has noticed: a $300 million raise at a $5 billion valuation in January 2026 (per Bloomberg), then a $1.5 billion Series F announced June 2026 at a reported $13 billion, on reported annualized revenue around $600 million.

Pricing is per minute of deployment uptime: the H100 is $0.10833/min ($6.50/hr), an A100 $4.00/hr, a B200 $9.98/hr, and an H100 MIG slice $3.75/hr, with the same rates for training and volume discounts advertised. Models deploy through Truss, its open-source packaging format, with autoscaling, canary deploys, and a Model APIs tier where hosted open-weights models (currently the Kimi K3 family and DeepSeek V4) bill per million tokens instead.

Which big GPU cloud is cheapest for H100 and B200? On each provider's own pricing page on November 3, 2026: for the H100, Crusoe at $3.90 per GPU-hour on demand, with Lambda a cent behind at $3.99 on an 8-GPU instance. For the B200, Lambda at $6.69 per GPU-hour (8x), well under Nebius ($8.50) and CoreWeave ($8.60). CoreWeave is the most expensive on demand, but if your job can be interrupted its published spot prices ($2.46 an H100, $4.26 a B200, per GPU) undercut everyone's on-demand rate. Two dates to know: Crusoe's own page says its H100 goes to $4.50 on December 1, 2026, which hands the cheapest on-demand H100 to Lambda.

results.title: Fireworks is raising on-demand GPU prices up to 30% on September 1 | Beyond the News
highlights:
# Fireworks is raising on-demand GPU prices up to 30% on September 1

Fireworks' current pricing table shows September 1 increases across H100, H200, B200, B300 and GB300 on-demand deployments, with B200 rising from $10 to $13 per GPU-hour. Dedicated training jobs that use the same GPU-hour rates inherit the new economics.

Reviewed and published by Lars Jansen Updated 28 Aug 2026, 10:59 pm NZST 4 min read Copy link

 First published 28 Aug 2026, 10:59 pm NZST 

## Key details

1. The new Fireworks on-demand GPU rates begin September 1, 2026.
2. H100 80GB: $7 → $8 per GPU-hour.
3. H200 141GB: $7 → $8 per GPU-hour.
4. B200 180GB: $10 → $13 per GPU-hour.
5. B300 288GB: $12 → $15 per GPU-hour.
6. GB300 288GB: $18 → $20 per GPU-hour.
7. On-demand deployments are billed per GPU second with no extra startup charges.
8. Region-restricted deployments are priced at a 1.5× premium.
9. Dedicated Training API jobs use the same on-demand GPU-hour pricing.

...

## What changed

Fireworks' current pricing page publishes a two-column transition for its on-demand GPU deployments: prices through August 31 and new rates from September 1, 2026. H100 80GB and H200 141GB increase from $7 to $8 per GPU-hour; B200 180GB rises from $10 to $13; B300 288GB from $12 to $15; and GB300 288GB from $18 to $20. Fireworks bills on-demand deployments per GPU second with no startup charge, and its Dedicated Training API uses the same GPU-hour pricing, so the change affects both dedicated serving and GPU-hour training jobs. Region-restricted deployments continue to carry a 1.5× premium.

## Why it matters

Dedicated GPU economics can dominate the unit cost of high-volume inference, fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning workloads. These increases range from roughly 11% to 30%, large enough to change break-even points between accelerator generations, serverless APIs and competing GPU clouds. The biggest increase is on B200, where a workload consuming 1,000 GPU-hours per month moves from $10,000 to $13,000 before regional premiums or other services. Teams should therefore benchmark completed-task throughput rather than choosing hardware on hourly price or peak specifications alone.

## The September increase varies materially by accelerator

H100 and H200 move from $7 to $8 per hour, about a 14.3% increase. B200 rises 30% from $10 to $13, B300 rises 25% from $12 to $15 and GB300 rises about 11.1% from $18 to $20. The uneven changes can alter the relative cost ranking of GPUs even when performance remains unchanged.

...

Fireworks states that Dedicated Training API jobs are priced per GPU hour using the On-Demand Pricing section. Teams running reinforcement fine-tuning or dedicated training should therefore update both serving and training forecasts, not only inference deployment budgets.

...

On-demand deployments are billed by the second and do not charge extra startup time, which remains useful for bursty workloads. But sustained fleets still absorb the full hourly increase, and a region-restricted deployment costs 1.5 times the listed rate.

## Hourly price is not total inference cost

A more expensive accelerator can still win if it materially improves throughput, latency or batch efficiency. Builders should compare cost per successful request, training run or completed agent task under the exact model, quantization, context and concurrency they use.

...

- The pricing page publishes the dated rate transition but does not explain the commercial rationale for each GPU-specific increase.
- Effective cost varies significantly with model serving efficiency, batching, quantization, context length and utilization.
- Enterprise or negotiated contracts may differ from public on-demand pricing.
